title: Recent sessions summary

commits.body: Brings the published traces up to this point: conversation that came after a session's last commit, and sessions with no commit of their own.

commits.summary: example-targets ready to launch: status working, and memory caps raised for the resized VM
commits.body: The push (prerequisite 7) was done, so the main brief's status is now working. The VM was resized from 28 vCPUs / 46 GiB to 30 vCPUs / 105 GiB. The 4G cap per feature loop OOM-killed processes 8 times during application-core (journalctl: reuse once, values four times, the merge loop three times on 2026-11-08), so each example-targets loop now gets 12G: the four stream briefs' '- memory:', a new '- memory: 12G' in the main brief, and the launch command's FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX (which overrides the briefs, as does ~/.profile, now also 12G). run-streams.sh's integration check scope goes from 3.5G to 6G. The runner's machine-local pipeline.local.toml (not committed) was rescaled to 13 workers, 26 CPUs, 76G, 24G per job and 8G for builds, which leaves about 34G for jobs while the four streams and the integration check run. Verified: bash -n on run-streams.sh, pipeline.py validate reports 0 problems, and the queue is empty.

commits.summary: Share the resized VM between feature loops, verification jobs and the user's terminals
commits.body: On the 30 vCPU / 105 GiB VM, 13 GiB and 2 vCPUs are now never handed out (the user's one or two Claude Code terminals, tmux and the background loops' own sessions, the OS and Docker, slack), leaving a pool of 92 GiB and 28 CPUs. Each feature loop takes its 12G cap and about 2 CPUs; the runner takes the rest. The run-verification skill's step 2 no longer describes only the 9 GB laptop: it tells the runner's agent to pick the row of the machine-local pipeline.local.toml's budget table that matches what is running (38G/18 CPUs/9 workers while run-streams.sh's streams run, 80G/26/13 with one loop, 92G/28/14 with none), and that file's [runner] defaults are the streams row, so a plain run is always safe even though a run keeps its budget until the queue empties and run-streams.sh starts the verification loop before the streams' scopes exist. feature-loop.sh's scope and run-streams.sh's integration-check scope now run at CPUWeight=50, so the user's terminals (weight 100, in the same user@ service) win when CPUs are contended; jobs were already held to their CPUQuota. Verified: CPUWeight=50 applies in a user scope on this machine (cpu.weight reads 50), bash -n on both scripts, pipeline.py loads 9 workers / 18 CPUs / 38 GiB from the local file, validate reports 0 problems, and each row adds up to 105 GiB and 30 CPUs.

commits.summary: Merged streams: regenerate the generated trace files, and check only the history of @
commits.body: Two false flags stopped work whenever feature-loop streams ran in parallel. First, every sync.py commit rewrites llm-dlc/index.json, traces/README.md, traces/metrics.json and README.md's session table, so once two streams had committed, run-streams.sh's integration check found the merge in conflict and never ran its script again (foundations, cleanup, application-core and example-targets all hit this; in foundations it hid a real serde bug until the merge), and every merge loop resolved the four files by hand. The new sync.py regenerate rewrites them from the per-session manifests and metrics, which sit in a directory per session and merge cleanly; it leaves and lists any other conflict, including one in README.md outside its index table, refuses if a session file itself conflicts, and exits 1 while anything is left. run-streams.sh's integration check now runs the merged tree's regenerate before deciding, and names what it regenerated in its report (installed by rename, so the running example-targets run keeps its old copy). The merge steps in engine-priorities.md (the worked example) and example-targets.md, and llm-dlc/README.md, now say to run it. Second, check_trailers read every commit in the repository with an LLM-Trace line, including other workspaces' lines, against this tree's manifests, so each stream's commits were reported as 'session ... has no manifest' everywhere else (26 errors today). It now reads ::@ only: a stream's commits are checked by its own commit in its workspace, and here once merged. Verified: new llm-dlc/tools/test_workspaces.py (7 tests, real jj repos with two workspaces: off-line commits not flagged, a bad trailer in this history still flagged, both lines checked after the merge, the four files settled, a README prose conflict and a session-file conflict reported; the off-line test fails with the old revset); test_review, test_runs, test_performance (103) and test_metrics pass. On real data, a scratch workspace merging the default line with the four example-targets streams' @- had all four files 5-sided in conflict; regenerate settled them (91 sessions), check then reported 0 errors once the streams' logs were copied in, as the reconcile does; and the integration script ran on the merge for the first time since the streams began committing (contract 14 pass, 2 skipped for want of a built jvmcontract; test_build, test_pipeline and build.py --plan pass), finding 3 runtime x workflow test errors described in the session. check in the default workspace now reports 0 errors (was 26).

commits.summary: Draft the stream-conductor brief: coordinate parallel streams during the run, not only at the merge
commits.body: A design for after example-targets is done: a fifth loop beside the streams that keeps a rolling, tested integration line (sync.py regenerate plus the integration script on every stream commit), routes integration failures and interface answers to per-stream inboxes instead of brief edits, settles decisions the brief delegates and queues the rest for the user with options and a recommendation, merges each stream as it finishes so its Phase 5 work starts at once, and takes over upkeep the user does today (clean-stop restarts, collecting warnings and allow-list proposals, telling a stream when a finding about it opens or closes). It is grounded in what the last four runs left for the end (foundations' hidden serde bug, cleanup's review session, application-core's seven interface requests and two late decisions, example-targets' build-route question and runtime x workflow disagreements), lists six implementation steps and five open decisions for the user, and is marked draft so nothing starts while the current loop runs. No code changed.

commits.summary: stream-conductor brief: the user's decisions folded in, with an act-first decision record
commits.body: The user settled the five open decisions directionally. The conductor decides when confident and when a decision is cheap to recover from or redo, and the user reviews afterwards rather than approving first. Design 3 now gives the test (confidence with a named basis; recovery cost cheap, costly or irreversible; a table of what to do with each pair; a never-delegated list; re-flagging as a decision's dependents grow, since recovery cost rises over time; an overturn flow that applies the recorded undo) and its tradeoffs. Notifications are deferred in favour of the data, so Design 4 defines one committed, append-only decision record per run (llm-dlc/decisions/NAME.jsonl, a schema checked by check) with generated projections: a review view, status-bar counts, inbox items and the merge loop's for-review list; the user reviews and answers by id through a small decisions.py. Early merge of a finished stream is a contextual judgement with stated criteria, never distracting the running streams; inboxes carry only what a stream has to act on; no rebase onto the integration line for now. The plan now starts with the decision record. Still a draft, to implement after example-targets is done; no code changed.
